title.narrative: National Social Safety Net Program-Scale Up

description.narrative: Expand coverage of shock responsive safety net support among the poor and vulnerable and strengthen the national safety net delivery system.

Nigeria's poverty numbers continue to rise due to persistently high inflation that has worsened since 2020 and reached a multi-decade high in early 2024. The number of poor people has increased from 80 million in 2018 to 109 million in 2023. In rural areas, the number of poor people increased by an estimated 14 percent over this period, whilst poverty in urban settings increased by 58 percent, as urban households are more exposed to inflation given that they consume own-produced food less frequently. Furthermore, households vulnerability to income shocks remains high, with about a quarter of households living on incomes 50 percent or less above the poverty line. The latest acceleration in prices started with COVID-19 and continued through early 2024. Inflation increased to 33.2 percent (yoy) in March 2024, driven by loose monetary conditions, the sharp depreciation of the naira in the parallel market, increases in the price of gasoline, and local supply constraints due to rising insecurity for agriculture production and transportation. External price shocks - such as the Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the severe floods in Q3-2022 - and import restrictions also contributed to the rise in inflation. The sluggish per capita growth and rising inflation are estimated to have increased poverty from 40 percent in 2018 to 49 percent in 2023.The government of Nigeria recognizing the urgency of improving the macroeconomic outlook and sustainably drive poverty reduction, undertook difficult but critical reforms. First, the government in May 2023 announced that it was ending the gasoline subsidy, and within days retail prices more than doubled. Although gasoline prices have now more than tripled since the end of 2022, they increased less than the rising import cost in local currency (naira) terms, as the naira in the official market has depreciated. Second, in June 2023, the government adopted a new FX policy whereby the multiple official FX rates were merged into a single official, market-reflective rate. New CBN leadership took office in September 2023 and, since then, additional progress has been made to implement the FX policy and address the premium between the now-unified official exchange rate and unofficial, parallel market rates, including by lifting the restriction on purchasing FX to import multiple products.Well-targeted cash transfers to the poor and vulnerable partially mitigate the adverse impacts of the gasoline subsidy removal, while institutional strengthening of social protection will sustain the shock-responsive system. The government's policy reforms, such as the reform of the gasoline subsidy, whilst vital for Nigeria's long-term poverty reduction prospects, may further worsen the poverty situation in the short-term without mitigation measures. The government is implementing a scaled-up cash transfer program, aiming to provide N75,000 to 15 million households. The World Bank is supporting the government's cash transfer program through the NASSP-SU project with a focus on providing targeted support to poor and economically insecure households in the social register, to protect the livelihoods of the existing chronically poor households as well as by strengthening the shock responsive national social protection system.Compared to the high levels of poverty and economic insecurity, the expenditures on safety nets and the coverage of safety net programs are low. In 2023, about 49 percent of Nigerians — 109 million people — were poor and an additional 47 million people were economically insecure and at high risk of falling into poverty. In addition to the short-term negative effects of the reforms, households are indirectly affected as the price increase is transmitted to other goods and services, especially through higher prices for transportation and electricity generation. Nigeria's social safety net programs have limited coverage of the poor and economically insecure. In 2018, only 17 percent of households were covered by any safety nets program and fewer than 1 percent were covered by any cash transfer program. In 2021, Nigeria spent only 0.14 percent of its GDP on social safety nets, much lower than the averages in Africa and lower middle-income countries of 1.2 percent. Even among those covered, benefit levels remain insufficient to keep households out of poverty. Furthermore, the social protection system remains fragmented despite the National Social Investment Programmes Act of 2023 and the National Social Protection Policy Framework.The overall objective of the NASSP SU is to expand coverage of shock responsive safety net support among the poor and vulnerable and strengthen the national safety net delivery system. Gender and citizen engagement are important dimension of the results to be achieved by the project. These will continue to be monitored through the outcome indicators as well as intermediate indicators looking at specific aspects of gender and citizen engagement.The project builds on the existing social protection systems supported under NASSP to provide strengthened social assistance support to Nigerian citizens and will support the following components:Component 1. Economic Shock Responsive Cash Transfer (ESR-CT). This component will provide temporary cash transfer to eligible beneficiaries in response to the current economic shocks affecting the country. The component has two subcomponents; i) Subcomponent 1.1. Rural ESR-CT to eligible beneficiaries in the NSR, ii) Subcomponent 1.2. Urban ESR-CT to eligible beneficiaries through the expansion of the RRR.Component 2. Extended Regular Cash Transfer (ER-CT) for the poor and the vulnerable. This component will provide social assistance to the poor and vulnerable by providing resources for a regular cash transfer program which commenced under the NASSP. As feasible, the regular cash transfer will be combined with a package of support services to improve the livelihood of the targeted households.Component 3. Delivery System Strengthening and Program management. Component 3 will expand and strengthen the social assistance/safety nets delivery systems through increased integration and use of digital technologies at various stages of the delivery chain and also provide project management support. The Component will support supports two subcomponents; I) Subcomponent 3.1. Expansion and strengthening of the safety nets delivery systems through increased integration and the use of digital technologies, I) Subcomponent 3.2. Project management support.In addition to the three-components discussed above, the project will also support: a) citizen engagement and social accountability, b) gender and social inclusion, an c) climate co-benefit, The primary beneficiaries of the project will be the cash transfer beneficiaries. In addition to cash transfer beneficiaries, the project will improve the delivery systems for social assistance programs – both current and future.The NASSP-SU project is aligned with the Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for the Federal Republic of Nigeria FY 21 – FY 25 (World Bank Report #153873-NG). The CPF has four strategic Pillars: (i) strengthening the foundations of the public sector; (ii) investing in human capital; (iii) promoting jobs and economic transformation and diversification; and (iv) enhancing resilience. The project will contribute to most of the pillars of the CPF. Most directly, the expansion of the CT programs contributes towards increasing the coverage and effectiveness of social assistance, a core objective under Pillar 2. It also contributes to other core objectives of improving investments in human capital under Pillar 2.
